It's a good question. From my view, there are three identifiable reasons.

First, there's the Valence Effect. If you give people a deck of 26 smiley face cards and 26 frowney face cards then ask them to predict the top card, they assess that there are greater than even odds of drawing a smiley face. There's an evolutionary advantage to assuming that good things will happen to a) keep spirits high, and b) be ready for opportunities as they arise. Since a typical person is completely unable to assess scientific truths, the decision appears to be drawing cards from a deck with an unknown number of each face. Might as well hope it's a good one.

Second, I think a lot of people see the world in strictly moral terms rather than probabilistic rational terms. If climate change is real, then everyone who has ever contributed to climate change is a bad person. Worse still, there is no alternative to contributing to the problem -- the only way to become a good person is to stop doing all the things that are harmful, which would involve destroying my life as I know it. I can't drive a car, so there's my job and ability to have transportation. I can't fly in a plane to visit my family. I can't shop at stores because that's the same as using the oil to make the products and ship them. Because things are either good or bad, any line of thinking that concludes cars, planes, and cheap underwear are bad must be a flawed line of thinking; otherwise, we would grind everything in our society to a halt. If climate change is real, the thinking goes, then all things contributing to it are evil - since these things are not evil, climate change must not be real. Another way this thinking can go is: things that I can't choose can't be evil, and I can't choose to stop heating the earth, therefore my actions are not evil and climate change is false. This thinking ignores the probabilistic effects of different activities and is stark contrast to the reality that even if we are changing the climate, some small change might not matter as long as the process can reach a stable point where the planet reaches a new homeostatis, i.e. stable temperatures and CO2 levels higher than the 1800s but below what they will be in 2050.

Third, I think there's just wanton ignorance mixed with an odd concoction of conspiracy theory and a kind of death wish for society. See whynotanon1's babble for a great example: Climate change is something to be argued because maybe if we argue properly then that will be a good substitute for science; or, maybe climate change is something someone is using to try to control me since that fits my model of how other people behave. This thinking is how climate change deniers are typically portrayed, e.g. it's still snowing so there isn't a problem.
